input.description: Fix #1196/#1197/#1203 gx_runner+run_service cluster
input.prompt:
Repo: DataQ (TheurgicDuke771/DataQ), a data-quality platform built on Great Expectations. Read CLAUDE.md in the repo root FIRST — it defines the mandatory per-functionality workflow (one branch/PR per functionality, tests, /code-review skill, push, PR, merge) and critical rules (never store metrics only in JSONB, redaction happens at the logger/read layer, PII redaction is load-bearing). Follow it exactly. This is a higher-stakes cluster (touches the redaction/security-adjacent path), so be careful and precise.

You have THREE related GitHub issues to fix, in this exact order, as three SEPARATE PRs, each fully merged before you start the next (so each PR's diff is clean and reviewable on its own, and so you're always branching from up-to-date main):

## 1. Issue #1196 (run first) — cap unexpected_index_list at capture time
Run `gh issue view 1196` for full text. Summary: `backend/app/datasources/gx_runner.py` calls GX with `result_format="COMPLETE"` everywhere (around lines 278, 286, 295). On the pandas execution engine (flat-file/ADLS/S3/Iceberg datasources), GX's `unexpected_index_list` comes back FULLY UNTRUNCATED under COMPLETE format (unlike the SQLAlchemy-backed engines, and unlike `partial_unexpected_list` which stays capped at ~20 rows / `partial_unexpected_count`). `_extract_sample_failures` (gx_runner.py:105-113) copies this list into `sample_failures` verbatim with no slicing anywhere in gx_runner.py or run_service.py. This means unbounded JSONB storage growth and unbounded API response size for `GET /runs/{id}` on large pandas-backed failures.
Fix: cap `unexpected_index_list` at capture time in `gx_runner._extract_sample_failures`, slicing to the same ~20-row cap `partial_unexpected_count` already gives elsewhere. Add a test asserting the captured list is bounded even when GX returns thousands of entries (pandas-backed fixture with a large failure count).

## 2. Issue #1197 (run second, after #1196 is merged and you've rebased) — redaction label undercount
Run `gh issue view 1197` for full text. Summary: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`'s `_RedactionTracker.record()` OR-accumulates a column's "was it shown" state across BOTH `unexpected_index_list` and `partial_unexpected_list` when both are present in one `sample_failures` payload. Each list is classified independently via `_known_sensitive`/`classify_column` (backend/app/services/column_classification.py, value-based heuristic over each list's OWN sample) — so the same column can classify "shown" against one list and "masked" against the other. Because the tracker ORs toward "shown", a column masked in `unexpected_index_list` (the list the frontend actually renders now, per already-merged PR #1190) but classified shown in `partial_unexpected_list` gets excluded from `redacted_columns` / undercounted in the `redaction` summary — even though every cell for that column in the DISPLAYED list reads "∎∎∎". This is a display-honesty bug (not a PII leak — whichever list is rendered has its own cells correctly masked), reopening the class #424/#1115 fixed.
Fix: since redaction state is computed read-time (#1115), make `redact_sample_failures`/`_RedactionTracker` classify/track against the SAME list the frontend displays: if a dict-shaped `unexpected_index_list` is present, track only from that list; otherwise track from `partial_unexpected_list` (keep existing #1115 anonymous-mask semantics for the scalar-list path). Add a regression test with a dual-list sample where the tested column masks in the index list but shows in the partial list — assert the label reflects the DISPLAYED (index) list. Keep the existing #1115 regression tests green.

## 3. Issue #1203 (run third, after #1197 is merged and you've rebased) — SQL exception leaks cell data into observed_value
Run `gh issue view 1203` for full text. Summary: `backend/app/services/run_service.py::_build_result` does `observed = {"error": outcome.error_message} if outcome.error_message else None` for an errored check. `outcome.error_message` is GX's `exception_info.exception_message` passed through verbatim. On a SQL execution engine (Snowflake, and now Unity Catalog via #1179), that's typically a SQLAlchemy `StatementError`, whose `str()` appends `[SQL: ...] [parameters: (...)]` — and warehouse cast/conversion errors commonly quote the offending CELL VALUE in the message itself (e.g. "Cannot parse '<value>' as INT"). This lands in `results.observed_value`, which is OUTSIDE the sample_failures retention sweep and OUTSIDE the suite's column-redaction policy — it reaches the run-detail API, UI, alerts, and MCP output completely unredacted. This is the same shape #989 already fixed for monitors (moving a cell value out of the message onto a structured field the read layer can redact).
Fix direction (per the issue, a design decision but with a clear suggested shape): strip the `[SQL: …] [parameters: …]` tail structurally — SQLAlchemy exposes `.statement`/`.params` separately on `StatementError`, so this is a structural strip (check `orig`/`statement`/`params` attributes), NOT a regex-on-prose hack — keep the driver's own first line of the message. Do NOT apply a blanket `classify_failure_reason`-style scrub (the issue explicitly warns this would regress usability — the message is often the most actionable diagnostic a user gets for a broken query; see `SafeMonitorError`'s docstring for why that distinction was drawn). Add a regression test: construct/simulate a `StatementError` carrying a parameter value, run it through `_build_result`, and assert the persisted `observed_value` does NOT contain that parameter value or the `[SQL:`/`[parameters:` tail, but DOES retain the driver's first-line message. This must work identically for both Snowflake and Unity Catalog (shared gx_runner/run_service path — no per-datasource divergence).

Workflow (repeat for EACH of the three, in order):
1. `conda activate dataq` (never `conda run` — it swallows stdin and fakes broken verdicts on this repo's tests).
2. `git checkout main && git pull` then `git checkout -b fix/issue-<N>-<slug>` off up-to-date main.
3. Implement the fix + tests as specified above.
4. Run Black/Ruff/mypy + the full affected test files locally (not just your new test) — confirm nothing else broke, especially the existing #1115/#989/#1190 regression tests mentioned above.
5. Commit (conventional commit, `Fixes #<N>`, `Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`), push, open PR (use `.github/pull_request_template.md`), milestone matching that issue's own milestone (`gh issue view <N> --json milestone`).
6. Run the `/code-review` skill (Skill tool, skill "code-review") on your diff — this cluster touches the redaction/security-sensitive path so take findings seriously. Fix blocking findings in a follow-up commit and push again. File a new GitHub issue for anything genuinely deferred (never drop silently, per CLAUDE.md's fixed-or-filed rule) — note in the PR/issue that it's a follow-up from this cluster.
7. Wait for CI green (`gh pr checks --watch`). Only squash-merge (`gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch`) if CI is green AND the code-review found nothing blocking. If code-review or CI surfaces something you're not confident fixing correctly, leave the PR open and say so clearly in your final report rather than merging something shaky — this path is security-adjacent.
8. Only THEN move to the next issue in the list.

At the end, report: for each of the 3 issues — PR URL, merge status (merged / open-and-why), and any follow-up issues filed. Be explicit about the #1197 and #1203 fixes' correctness reasoning since they're the trickiest.

Gotchas: shell may be fish (quote glob flags, no `timeout` binary — don't use it). Never `--no-verify`, never force-push. Don't drop a finding silently — every review finding ends fixed or filed.

input.description: Fix #1101 phantom delivered-first stamp
input.prompt:

Summary: `publish_connection_health` in `backend/app/worker/tasks.py` sets `connections.health_alerted_at` whenever `CompositePublisher.publish_health` returns without raising. But every real channel (Teams/Slack/email) returns `None` when unconfigured, and the composite never raises in that case — so on a workspace with zero alert channels configured (the shipped default), a connection-health FAILING edge stamps `health_alerted_at` with ZERO notifications actually sent. Apply the identical contract to `publish_health`: the per-connection path claims the flag with a conditional UPDATE BEFORE dispatching the send task (per #842/#843) — so your fix belongs in `publish_connection_health`'s post-publish bookkeeping: release the claim on an undeliverable publish, mirroring the existing publish-failed path. Write tests specifically around the #842 claim/release flow (a workspace with zero configured channels must NOT stamp `health_alerted_at`; a workspace with a configured channel that actually sends must still stamp it).

input.description: Fix #1109 lineage first-call abort
input.prompt:
Repo: DataQ (TheurgicDuke771/DataQ). Read CLAUDE.md in the repo root first for the mandatory per-functionality workflow (branch → implement → tests → /code-review skill → push → PR → merge). Follow it exactly.

Task: fix GitHub issue #1109. Run `gh issue view 1109` for full text. Summary: `SnowflakeLineageProvider._from_get_lineage` classifies the FIRST `GET_LINEAGE` call's failure through `_reraise_if_feature_unsupported`: an edition gate (`0A000`) or grant denial becomes `_FeatureUnsupportedError` and the tier ladder descends to ACCESS_HISTORY / OBJECT_DEPENDENCIES. Anything else re-raises, and since `fetch_edges` only catches `_FeatureUnsupportedError`, the WHOLE pull fails — including lower tiers that would have answered fine. This behavior is deliberate/pinned for the pre-existing single-probe case (test `test_an_unclassified_failure_on_the_first_call_still_aborts_the_pull` exists and encodes it), but the per-seed traversal (#892) now makes up to 2×N calls (N = `WAREHOUSE_LINEAGE_MAX_SEEDS`, default 500) — so a transient blip on call 1 of 1000 now costs the entire graph.

Fix shape (per the issue): treat an unclassified first-call failure the same way seed-enumeration failures are already treated — skip that tier with a classified reason (e.g. `"get_lineage: call failed: <ExceptionType>"`) and let the union of remaining tiers answer, instead of raising. Critical constraint: do NOT fold this into a CONFIDENT EMPTY at the top tier (that would incorrectly prune a lower tier's real graph) — descending must be the only effect. Also critical: the FLOOR tier's own total failure must still raise `WarehouseLineageUnavailableError` — a total denial must never silently read as an empty graph. The classified reason must carry the exception TYPE only, never raw connector text (the #902 rule — check that rule before writing the reason string).

Required test: a regression test with a poison/unclassified error injected on call 1 of a multi-seed traversal, asserting it descends to the union instead of raising, and that `skipped_tiers` carries the classified reason. Also update/replace the existing pinned test `test_an_unclassified_failure_on_the_first_call_still_aborts_the_pull` since its asserted behavior is exactly what you're changing — rename/rewrite it to assert the NEW (descend, not abort) behavior, and note in your commit why the old pin is being flipped.

Workflow:
1. `conda activate dataq` (never `conda run`).
2. Branch: `git checkout -b fix/issue-1109-lineage-first-call-abort`.
3. Implement + tests as above. Find the relevant lineage provider file (search for `_from_get_lineage`, `_reraise_if_feature_unsupported`, `fetch_edges` under `backend/app/`).
4. Run Black/Ruff/mypy + the full lineage test suite locally (not just your new test).

input.prompt:

- [ ] Toggling away mid-walk stops further page requests — test: mock N pages, toggle away after page 1 resolves, assert no further fetch calls happen.

- [ ] Rapid toggling produces at most one in-flight walk at a time.

input.description: Build #1202 custom-SQL metric_value
input.prompt:
Repo: DataQ (TheurgicDuke771/DataQ). Read CLAUDE.md in the repo root first for the mandatory per-functionality workflow (branch → implement → tests → /code-review skill → push → PR → merge), AND note CLAUDE.md §10's critical rule: "metric_value is the SQL-aggregatable scalar a monitor measured; don't store metrics only in JSONB observed_value." Follow CLAUDE.md exactly.

Task: implement GitHub issue #1202 (needs a deliberate design decision, per the issue). Run `gh issue view 1202` for full text, and read ADR 0019 (`docs/adr/0019-*.md` — find the exact filename) for the existing custom-SQL check design, plus the already-merged severity/metric_value seam (grep `severity.extract_metric` under `backend/app/`).

Summary: a custom-SQL check (ADR 0019) produces a genuine scalar — the unexpected row count — but it lands ONLY in JSONB: `observed_value = {"observed_value": 74}`. `metric_value` stays NULL on both Snowflake and Unity Catalog. ADR 0019 §4 deliberately chose binary pass/fail for "this query should return no rows" (correct, don't change that), but the row count itself is never captured as a bandable metric, so: the per-check metric trend view (#594) has nothing to plot for custom-SQL checks, an `anomaly` monitor can't baseline against it, and "is this rule getting worse?" is unanswerable in SQL.

Scope (per the issue, this is EXACT — follow it, don't improvise beyond it):
- Populate `metric_value` from the unexpected row count in `gx_runner`/`severity.extract_metric` for `unexpected_rows_expectation`, on BOTH datasources (Snowflake and Unity Catalog) at once — a per-datasource divergence would make the same check band differently depending on where it runs. This is an ADDITIVE change in `severity.extract_metric` — ADR 0019 §Consequences already confirms "no schema change" (the `metric_value` column already exists per the Week-3 threshold migration, per CLAUDE.md §10 — do NOT add a migration).
- Decide the semantic DELIBERATELY: a raw row count is not comparable across tables of different sizes — decide whether the bandable quantity should be the raw count, or a percentage of the batch (which costs a second aggregate query). Make this decision explicitly and document your reasoning in the PR description; don't just pick silently.
- CRITICAL constraint: existing rows keep `metric_value = NULL` — do NOT backfill a guess.
- CRITICAL constraint: thresholds are already optional on a check — adding a metric must NOT turn today's binary (no-threshold) checks into something that bands unexpectedly. A check with no thresholds configured must keep resolving EXACTLY as it does today (pass/fail only, no band). Write a test specifically proving this: a no-threshold custom-SQL check with unexpected_rows > 0 still resolves as a simple fail with no severity band applied, even though `metric_value` is now populated.

Required tests: `metric_value` gets populated with the chosen semantic on both Snowflake and Unity Catalog paths (mock/fixture both); a check WITH thresholds now bands correctly against the new metric; a check WITHOUT thresholds is unaffected (see constraint above); existing/old rows with NULL `metric_value` are left alone (no backfill logic exists).

1. `conda activate dataq` (never `conda run`).
2. Branch: `git checkout -b feature/issue-1202-custom-sql-metric-value`.
3. Implement in `severity.extract_metric` (or wherever the ADR points) + tests as above.
4. Run Black/Ruff/mypy + relevant tests (severity, gx_runner, both datasource run-path tests) locally.

### Candidate 1 — psycopg2 `connect_timeout` doesn't bound pooled/reused connections

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

The mechanics check out against documented behavior, and this doesn't require a live network-partition test to establish — it follows deterministically from how libpq and SQLAlchemy's pool are specified to work:

- **psycopg2/libpq `connect_timeout`** is a libpq connection parameter. It only bounds the time from socket-open through the connection reaching `CONNECTION_OK` (TCP handshake + auth). Once `create_engine()`'s `connect_args` produces a live DBAPI connection and it's returned to the pool, `connect_timeout` has no further effect on that connection — it is not re-applied to reads/writes on an already-open socket, and psycopg2 does not translate it into an ongoing `SO_RCVTIMEO`/socket read timeout.
- **`pool_pre_ping=True`** in SQLAlchemy runs `dialect.do_ping(dbapi_connection)` on checkout — for the psycopg2/postgres dialect this executes a cursor query (effectively `SELECT 1`) on the **existing pooled DBAPI connection object**. This is not a call to `connect()`, so `connect_timeout` is architecturally out of scope for it.
- No `statement_timeout` GUC is set (the file's own comment explicitly says this is deliberate, to not cap legitimate long-running GX queries), and no psycopg2 socket-level keepalive args (`keepalives`, `keepalives_idle`, `keepalives_interval`, `keepalives_count`) are set either — those would be the mechanism that lets the OS detect a silently-dead peer on an idle/in-use socket. Their absence corroborates the gap.
- On a routing-level partition with no RST/ICMP-unreachable, a blocking read on that socket is bounded only by the OS's TCP retransmission timeout (Linux default `tcp_retries2` ≈ 15, commonly 13–30 min depending on RTT) — large and effectively "the same order of unboundedness" the PR set out to eliminate, not the ~10s the fix advertises.

So the reasoning is sound: the fix genuinely narrows the **first-connect** case (a DB that's unreachable *before* the app ever talks to it — cold start, or a connection recycled after `pool_pre_ping` detects and discards a dead one) but does **not** protect a connection that was healthy, is sitting checked-out or idle in the pool, and goes silent mid-life. The file's own comment ("a dead DB fails fast and loudly instead of hanging every caller") overclaims relative to that scope — "every caller" is true only for callers needing a *new* connection, not ones reusing a pooled one. For the specific #1052 staleness-loop shutdown scenario named in the PR, if the partition happens after the loop's connection is already established and pooled, the graceful-shutdown await can still hang for OS-timeout-scale duration.

input.description: Fix #1109 regression finding, then merge
input.prompt:
Repo: DataQ. A prior agent session was interrupted by an account spend-limit error mid-task. Resume the work — do NOT start over, and do NOT just merge as-is.

Existing state: `cd /Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/.claude/worktrees/agent-af26f477cbdfa98de` — existing git worktree, branch `fix/issue-1109-lineage-first-call-abort`, PR **#1220** already open (`gh pr view 1220`), CI all green (14/14). Read CLAUDE.md in that worktree's root first.

Background: issue #1109 (`gh issue view 1109`) is about `SnowflakeLineageProvider._from_get_lineage` in `backend/app/lineage/warehouse_snowflake.py` — an unclassified error on the FIRST `GET_LINEAGE` call used to abort the whole pull; the fix makes it descend to lower tiers instead (skip just that tier, classified reason, let the union answer), since the per-seed traversal now makes up to 2N calls and a transient blip on call 1 shouldn't cost the whole graph.

**A `/code-review` pass already ran on this PR before the session was interrupted, and found a real, substantive regression that was NOT yet fixed.** Read the PR's existing state (`git log -p` on this branch vs main, and `gh pr view 1220 --json body,comments`) to see the current diff. The key finding to address:

**The core problem:** swallowing the unclassified first-call GET_LINEAGE failure and treating it as a degraded-but-successful result means `fetch_edges` returns a normal `WarehouseLineageResult` instead of raising. That result flows through `_persist` in `backend/app/lineage/warehouse_refresh.py`, which — since `SnowflakeLineageProvider.is_incremental` is False — PRUNES the snapshot's `lineage_edges` down to just the floor/ACCESS_HISTORY tier for that cycle, on EVERY transient GET_LINEAGE blip. This directly contradicts `warehouse_refresh.py`'s own documented "#828 never-prune-on-unavailable" invariant (a transient blip should never wipe previously-cached richer edges). Additionally, `refresh_connection_lineage` clears `connection.lineage_last_error` to None and counts the connection as "refreshed" on this degraded path — understating a real recurring problem.

Secondary findings from the review (address if you can do so cleanly, otherwise file follow-up issues — don't let scope balloon and block the primary fix):
- The fix is ordinal-based (only call #1 is protected) — calls 2..2N-1 failing unclassified still silently fold into `seed_failures` with a bare structlog line and no product-visible signal, even for a majority-failure run. This is PRE-EXISTING (from #892), not introduced by this PR, but the PR touches exactly this code path — per CLAUDE.md's "don't dismiss pre-existing findings" rule, this needs at minimum a filed follow-up issue if not fixed here.
- If the floor tier ALSO fails after an unclassified first-call GET_LINEAGE failure, the original GET_LINEAGE failure detail is discarded before `fetch_edges` raises `WarehouseLineageUnavailableError` — no test covers this combined-failure case.
- Minor: `f"call failed ({type(exc).__name__})"` doesn't distinguish "transient, may self-heal next cycle" from "structurally unsupported, permanent" in the UI-facing degraded_reason text.

**Your job:** decide and implement the RIGHT fix for the primary pruning-regression problem. The likely correct shape: when a tier is skipped due to an UNCLASSIFIED failure (as opposed to a classified `_FeatureUnsupportedError` like an edition gate or grant denial, which IS a legitimate "this tier will never work" signal), the result should be treated as non-authoritative for pruning purposes — i.e. `_persist` should NOT prune previously-cached tier data on a transient-unclassified-skip, only on a classified/confirmed-unsupported skip or a genuine confident-empty. You'll need to thread some signal (e.g. a flag or a distinct classification on `WarehouseLineageResult`/`skipped_tiers`) from `_from_get_lineage` through `fetch_edges` to `_persist` distinguishing "transient, don't prune" from "confirmed unsupported, prune is fine." Look at how `is_incremental`/prune logic currently works in `_persist` to find the right hook point. Also fix (or explicitly decide not to, with reasoning) the `lineage_last_error`/refresh-count understatement.

Write regression tests: (1) an unclassified first-call failure does NOT prune previously-cached GET_LINEAGE-tier edges on the next persist cycle (only degrades the read for that cycle); (2) a genuinely classified `_FeatureUnsupportedError` first-call failure (edition gate etc.) still allows normal pruning to the lower tier, since that's a legitimate permanent state; (3) the combined GET_LINEAGE+floor failure case still raises `WarehouseLineageUnavailableError` with useful diagnostic info.

2. Implement the fix on the existing branch. Re-run the FULL lineage test suite (not just new tests) plus `warehouse_refresh` tests to confirm nothing else broke.
3. Run Black/Ruff/mypy locally.
4. Commit as a follow-up commit on the same branch (conventional commit describing the prune-regression fix), push.
5. Re-run the `/code-review` skill on the UPDATED diff to confirm the fix actually addresses the finding and didn't introduce new issues. File GitHub issues for the secondary findings above if you didn't fix them in this PR (use the fixed-or-filed rule — don't drop them).

7. Report: PR URL, merge status, exactly what you changed to fix the pruning regression, what you did about the secondary findings (fixed vs filed, with issue numbers), and your confidence level.

## Findings

**Angle 1 — Altitude**

1. `_FLATFILE_TYPES` in `backend/app/services/run_target.py` (lines 128–131, 158–162) is dead-weight duplication, not a justified special case. Traced the actual call path: `preview_batch` → `resolve_target` → `resolve_target_shape` (`backend/app/datasources/registry.py:357`) → `_TARGET_RESOLVERS`. That registry has no entry for `adf`/`airflow` (raises `TargetShapeError("...has no run path...")`) and its `snowflake`/`unity_catalog`/`iceberg` resolvers all call `_require(target, "table", conn_type)`, which already raises `TargetShapeError` because a batch-shaped `{pattern, strategy, prefix}` dict has no `table` key. So for every connection type the guard rejects, `resolve_target` — called two lines later in the very same function — would already raise the equivalent `SuiteTargetInvalidError`. The guard only changes the error string, not the outcome. Its own comment ("duplicated ... rather than imported so this module's write-time validation path stays GX-free") is also empirically false: `run_target.py:43` already does `from backend.app.datasources.registry import resolve_target_shape` unconditionally at module load, and `registry.py` already does `from backend.app.datasources.flatfile import build_flatfile_runner` unconditionally at module load, and `flatfile.py:39` does `import great_expectations as gx` at module load — so importing `run_target` (which `suite_service`'s write path already does) has been loading GX transitively all along, pre-existing this PR. The stated GX-avoidance rationale doesn't hold, so there's no justification left for hand-duplicating the type set instead of calling `resolve_target_shape` directly and mapping its (already-correct) `TargetShapeError`/`SuiteTargetInvalidError`.

2. The three new error classes (`BatchPreviewNoDataError`, `BatchPreviewInvalidError`, `BatchPreviewFailedError`) and their try/except mapping live in the **router** (`backend/app/api/v1/suites.py:517–529, 561–589`). Every sibling no-persistence preview endpoint does the opposite: `dry_run_check` (`backend/app/api/v1/checks.py:452`) has zero try/except and is a pure pass-through to `dryrun_service.dry_run_check`, whose own module (`backend/app/services/dryrun_service.py:51,56,...`) defines `DryRunUnsupportedError`/`DryRunNoDataError`/`DryRunFailedError` and does the identical `BatchNotFoundError→422 / DataQError passthrough / Exception→502 w/ classify_failure_reason` translation internally. `profile_columns` (`suites.py:426`) is the same: `ProfileUnsupportedError` etc. live in `profile_service.py:91–113`, and the router has no try/except at all. This is an inconsistency in where error taxonomy is owned — a future service-layer caller of `preview_batch` (not the HTTP router) gets undifferentiated `ValueError`s instead of typed `DataQError`s the way every other service in this codebase behaves.

## Summary

The diff's core complexity driver is a design choice made in an earlier PR (#1186): `workspace_health.key` is a bare SHA-256-derived hash with no sibling detail column (justified by the 64-char PK cap vs 256-char Airflow DAG ids). PR #1235's read side has to work around that by reconstructing candidate tuples and hash-probing for hits, which creates a real coupling: the write side (`orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses`) derives tuples from one known `run_env` crossed against enabled bindings with a *different* env; the read side (`list_current_env_near_misses`) has to invert that — it doesn't know `run_env`, so it must enumerate all *other* `ENVS` members as candidates per binding. Both sides must agree on `_near_miss_key`'s exact field order/format forever, silently and without an error path if they ever drift (a mismatch just yields empty results, not a failure). This complexity is inherent to the opaque-hash storage decision, and a `NearMissRecord` dataclass + `NearMissRead` Pydantic model both duplicate the same 5-field shape across layers (normal, but worth noting).

Frontend: `nearMisses: TriggerEnvNearMiss[]` is threaded through `TriggersPanel → TriggersBody → TriggerRow`, doing a linear `.find()` per row inside the `renderItem` callback (recomputed every render).

Findings:

1. **file:** `backend/app/services/workspace_health_service.py:155-230` (`list_current_env_near_misses`)
   **summary:** Read side re-derives every one of `enabled_bindings × (len(ENVS)-1)` candidate tuples and hashes each to probe for a stored row, duplicating (in inverted form) the tuple-generation logic that `orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses` already owns.
   **failure_scenario:** If `_near_miss_key`'s field composition/order ever changes on one side without the other (or `ENVS` gains a member), lookups silently return empty — no exception, no test failure signal beyond a behavioral gap. Storing the decoded `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, run_env, binding_env)` as real columns in a small dedicated `trigger_env_near_miss` table (composite PK, `pipeline_or_dag_id` as unbounded `Text`, avoiding the 64-char cap that forced hashing in the first place) turns this into one `SELECT ... WHERE updated_at >= cutoff`, eliminates the hash-guess loop entirely, and removes the two-implementation coupling.

2. **file:** `backend/db/models.py:1248` (root cause) / `backend/app/services/workspace_health_service.py:210-224` (`_near_miss_key`)
   **summary:** The underlying design constraint (opaque hash, no detail column, driven by `WorkspaceHealth.key`'s shared 64-char PK) is what forces the guess-and-check read pattern.
   **failure_scenario:** A dedicated near-miss table (or a JSONB detail column alongside the existing hash key, keeping the hash as dedupe PK but adding `payload: dict` for decode) would let the read side just deserialize instead of reconstructing. Saves the `O(bindings × 3)` hash computation per request and the entire candidate-dict bookkeeping (`candidates: dict[str, tuple[...]]`, lines 196-207).

3. **file:** `frontend/src/components/suites/TriggersPanel.tsx:684-689`
   **summary:** `TriggerRow`'s near-miss match is a `.find()` over the full `nearMisses` array inside the `renderItem` callback, re-run on every render of every row.
   **failure_scenario:** Building one `Map<string, TriggerEnvNearMiss>` keyed by `` `${provider}|${pipeline_or_dag_id}|${binding_env}` `` once in `TriggersPanel` (via `useMemo`) and passing a single looked-up `nearMiss` (or the map itself) down would replace N `.find()` calls with N `Map.get()` calls and centralize the matching key logic in one place instead of inline in JSX — low-severity given the array is tiny (≤3× enabled bindings), but the pattern doesn't scale and obscures the match semantics at the call site.

4. **file:** `frontend/src/components/suites/TriggersPanel.tsx:641-676` (prop threading)
   **summary:** `nearMisses` is threaded as a raw prop through `TriggersPanel → TriggersBody → TriggerRow`, three layers deep, purely to be matched per-row at the bottom.
   **failure_scenario:** Minor — this is idiomatic React and the tree is shallow, so it's a low-priority nit rather than a real problem; flagged only because combining it with finding #3 (do the matching once at the `TriggersBody` level, pass each row its resolved `nearMiss` via a memoized map lookup rather than passing the whole array down) removes both the drilling-for-raw-data smell and the per-row linear scan in one change.

**Not flagged as issues:** the fail-open `nearMissState.status === 'ok' ? ... : []` resilience pattern, the `since_hours` recency window, and the `NearMissRecord`/`NearMissRead` dual-model split are reasonable and idiomatic for this codebase's layering conventions.</result>

<result>## Assessment

This is a real altitude problem, not a nitpick. `workspace_health`'s own docstring frames it as a **write-only delivered-alert/dedupe flag** (`key` + `alerted_at` + `updated_at`, no payload) — a shape that's fine for "has this been sent" but was never designed to answer "what business tuple does this row represent." The PR needs exactly that second question and answers it by re-implementing the write side's candidate-generation logic on the read side and using it as an oracle against opaque hashes. The hash function itself (`_near_miss_key`) *is* shared code, so that part can't drift. But the **candidate-selection logic** — which `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, run_env, binding_env)` tuples are even eligible to be hashed — exists in two places (`orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses` and `workspace_health_service.list_current_env_near_misses`), tied together only by a prose comment, not a shared function or a shared test. The new tests exercise the read side against the low-level write leaf (`record_trigger_binding_env_near_miss`), never against the actual production write path (`_record_env_near_misses`), so a change to that derivation logic would ship green and desync silently in prod. `ENVS` is at least a shared imported constant with a DB check constraint on both sides, so the "new env added" risk is lower than it first appears — the sharper risk is any future change to the *selection* logic (scoping, extra conditions, disabled-connection handling), which has zero compiler/test coupling. The "no schema change" checkbox is a false economy: a `detail` JSONB column or a dedicated `trigger_env_near_misses` table would have made the read trivial and change-safe, at the cost of one migration this PR explicitly avoided.

description: In-progress multi-PR sweep fixing all fixable GitHub issues numbered >1000; RESUME FROM HERE next session — worktrees, agent state, and per-PR blockers below

Session 2026-08-08 evening/night: triaged all 19 open GitHub issues numbered >1000 on TheurgicDuke771/DataQ, excluded 3 (see below), and ran 16 issues through the full CLAUDE.md workflow (branch → implement → test → `/code-review` → PR → merge) via many parallel background agents, each in its own git worktree under `.claude/worktrees/agent-<id>/`. **Session hit the account monthly spend limit once mid-flight** (multiple agents killed by API error) — recovered by having the user raise the cap and resuming; all WIP was safely committed to worktrees before the interruption, nothing was lost. **This session is ending before the sweep fully completes** — remaining work below.

**Excluded from the sweep entirely (do not re-attempt without a fresh decision):**
- **#1118** (SSRF via `*_secret_name`) — deliberately deferred to the RBAC epic (#740–#744) per the issue's own text.
- **#1030, #1032** (harness dbt GRANT hook / password-auth in deployed harness Terraform) — need a live Snowsight GRANT + Terraform apply against currently-stopped harness infra; not safe to do unattended.

## Fully merged this session (11 issues, done — no action needed)
#1195 (PR #1215), #1200 (PR #1217), #1102 (PR #1216, extended to `backend/alembic/env.py`; follow-up **#1221** filed for a pooled-connection connect_timeout gap, not yet picked up), #1101 (PR #1225 — found+fixed a real bug: `dispatch.py` ignored `publish_health`'s bool return), #1205 (PR #1218 + docs PR #1232), #1107 (PR #1224 — review found+fixed a real bug: `AssetsTableView` never forwarded the abort signal to `listAssets`), #1001 (PR #1222 + docs PR #1237 — review found+fixed a **real regression**: the `RangeReader` chunk size for Parquet sampling was so small it transferred *more* bytes than the whole-object download it was meant to replace, 6.8x amplification measured), #1196 (PR #1219, part of the #1196→#1197→#1203 cluster), #1109 (PR #1220 — review found+fixed a **real correctness regression**: the fix as first drafted caused every transient GET_LINEAGE blip to prune previously-cached richer lineage edges down to the coarse fallback tier, contradicting the codebase's own "#828 never-prune-on-unavailable" invariant; fixed via a `WarehouseLineageResult.prunable` flag threaded through `_persist`; **a second review round then caught the fix's own inversion bug** — mutation-tested, 8/8 killed; follow-ups **#1228** and **#1236** filed).

## Still open — RESUME HERE, in priority order

### #1197 → PR #1238 (`fix/issue-1197-redaction-tracks-displayed-list`)
Second issue in the #1196/#1197/#1203 cluster. PR is open; status when session ended unknown (agent was still running via SendMessage-reachable subagent `a51c0d9ca6de9dc1a`, part of the delegator agent `af2f53115f04dd0fb`'s original chain — check `gh pr checks 1238` and `gh pr view 1238 --json mergeStateStatus`). Worktree: `.claude/worktrees/agent-af2f53115f04dd0fb` (branch now `fix/issue-1197-redaction-tracks-displayed-list`). **After this merges, #1203 (SQL exception cell-data leak into `observed_value`, bypassing column redaction) still needs to be started from scratch** — it's the third and most security-relevant issue in this cluster, not yet begun. Full spec was given to the original delegator agent; re-read `gh issue view 1203` and the earlier session's agent prompt pattern (fix `_build_result` in `run_service.py` to strip `[SQL: …][parameters: …]` structurally via SQLAlchemy `.statement`/`.params`, not regex).

### #1199 → PR #1235 (`feature/issue-1199-near-miss-surfacing`)
CI fully green (14/14). `/code-review` found several real, non-trivial findings **not yet addressed**:
1. **Access-control widening (most important):** `GET /orchestration/near-misses` is auth-only/workspace-wide unscoped, but `TriggerBinding` rows are suite-owned config that `GET /trigger-bindings` already suite-scopes. This PR lets any authenticated user enumerate trigger-binding info for suites they don't own — a real new exposure, not precedented by the `/orchestration/pipelines` analogy the PR's docstring cites.
2. Frontend badge only shows the FIRST matching near-miss when multiple are concurrently current for the same binding (`.find()`, no dedup) — could hide a second live mismatch.
3. No `ORDER BY` on the `WorkspaceHealth` read query before the Python-side sort — result ordering isn't guaranteed on ties.
4. Disabling a binding (`onChanged`) doesn't refresh `nearMissState`, so a stale mismatch badge can persist until the panel remounts.
5. New tests exercise the write **leaf** (`record_trigger_binding_env_near_miss`) not the actual production write path (`_record_env_near_misses`) — a future change to candidate-selection logic could silently desync read/write with all tests green (echoes this codebase's own retro lesson about tests that can't express the failing case).
Agent to resume: `aad4dc92855562318` (may still be reachable via `SendMessage`/`ListAgents`). Worktree: `.claude/worktrees/agent-a2335f5ca668e9525` (branch `feature/issue-1199-near-miss-surfacing`).

### #1193 → PR #1233 (`feature/issue-1193-batch-target-preview`)
Review found one real, worth-fixing-before-merge issue: the `except (BatchListingTooLargeError, ValueError)` clause in the new `preview_batch_target` endpoint (`backend/app/api/v1/suites.py`) echoes raw `str(exc)` straight into the client-facing error envelope — every other similar endpoint in the codebase (`dryrun_service.py` etc.) routes unexpected exceptions through `classify_failure_reason()` specifically because adapter exceptions can carry DSN/credential fragments. Fix: narrow the clause to just `BatchListingTooLargeError` (safe fixed string) and let bare `ValueError` fall through to the generic `except Exception` → `classify_failure_reason` 502 path. Also flagged (non-blocking, worth folding in): `_FLATFILE_TYPES` in `run_target.py` duplicates a check `resolve_target()` already performs two lines later (its "keeps this GX-free" rationale is factually false — GX is already transitively imported), and the new error classes live in the router instead of the service layer (diverges from the `dryrun_service`/`profile_service` sibling pattern). Worktree: `.claude/worktrees/agent-afa1a98eee1196ff1`.

### #1108 → PR #1231 (`fix/issue-1108-paging-totals`)
Review found (non-blocking but worth a look): `/runs` and `/pipeline_runs` don't validate `status` against a closed vocabulary (unlike `/incidents`'s `state`, which 422s) — a typo'd/wrong-case status silently returns a confident empty result, the exact #828 pattern this codebase explicitly guards against elsewhere. Also: no composite index backing the new `(created_at, id)` tie-break ordering on `runs` (perf concern under deep offset paging, relevant given this ships under the "scale-aware execution" W6 milestone); `count_*`/`list_*` pairs duplicate filter logic by hand (drift risk); pre-existing low-severity TOCTOU between count and list queries (same pattern as `/assets`, not a regression). Worktree: `.claude/worktrees/agent-aef7256da7da527b1`.

### #1104 → PR #1227 (`fix/issue-1104-inventory-sync-visibility`)
**Highest-priority remaining item — review found real robustness bugs, not style nits:**
1. Unguarded `session.commit()` inside the per-connection `except` block (and the mirrored one in the success `else` branch) — if that bookkeeping commit itself fails (transient Postgres error), the exception is uncaught and aborts the **entire nightly sweep** for every remaining connection, violating the function's own documented "one broken connection never starves the rest" contract.
2. Missing row-lock on `inventory_sync_failing_since` — plain read-modify-write, a lost-update race under concurrent sweeps. The codebase has an **exact documented precedent** for this (`orchestration_service.record_poll_failure`'s `consecutive_poll_failures`, explicitly `with_for_update`-locked) that this PR didn't follow.
3. Reads `connection.type`/other attributes immediately after `session.rollback()` without re-fetching — attributes are expired on rollback, so a concurrent connection-delete mid-sweep raises uncaught `ObjectDeletedError`, again aborting the whole sweep. `record_poll_failure`'s own docstring documents this exact hazard in this exact codebase and re-fetches deliberately.
4. `classify_inventory_sync_error`'s broad substring-based PERMISSION classification can misdiagnose an unrelated failure (e.g. a secret-store outage reading the credential before the warehouse is ever touched) as "missing SELECT grant", sending an admin to fix the wrong thing while the real problem (e.g. Key Vault/OpenBao access) stays undiagnosed.
5. Minor: `inventory_sync_last_error`/`_failing_since` never clear when a connection opts OUT of `inventory_sync` — can go permanently stale if re-enabled later. Also several non-blocking duplication/simplification nits versus the `refresh_connection_lineage`/`orchestration_service` precedents.
Agent to resume: `a39e8e5d66bcc5b0e`. Worktree: `.claude/worktrees/agent-ae58b2b196e16a9a0` (branch `fix/issue-1104-inventory-sync-visibility`, includes a migration `c22fa93eb834_add_connection_inventory_sync_state.py` — test up+down before merging per CLAUDE.md's migration checklist).

### #1202 → PR #1223 (`feature/issue-1202-custom-sql-metric-value`)
Review came back **fully clean** across bug-scan, git-history, CLAUDE.md-compliance, and code-comment-compliance passes — only one cosmetic nit (a stale comment in `backend/app/datasources/base.py` claiming GX-expectation metrics always come "from the sample", now inaccurate for the custom-SQL `observed_value` path). **However, `gh pr view 1223` now shows `mergeStateStatus: DIRTY`** — it has fallen behind `main` from all the concurrent merges this session and needs a rebase/merge-main before it can merge. Should be the fastest one to close out. Worktree: `.claude/worktrees/agent-a24f7cde1eaa453aa`.

### #1234 (docs-only, `docs/progress-1225-snapshot`)
A docs follow-up PR for #1101/#1225's Snapshot recount, opened but not confirmed merged — low priority, safe to merge once CI is green if nothing else has since made its counts stale (check with `gh issue list` and re-derive the count fresh rather than trusting this PR's numbers, since many other PRs merged after it was opened).

Do this LAST, once, after all PRs above are settled, not per-PR.

If none are reachable, each worktree above still has its full commit history — read `git log -p` on the branch before re-implementing anything.

## Task 1: finish and merge PR #1238 (fixes #1197)
Work in the existing worktree at /Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/.claude/worktrees/agent-af2f53115f04dd0fb, branch fix/issue-1197-redaction-tracks-displayed-list. This PR already has CI fully green (14/14 checks) but has NOT yet had a `/code-review` pass run against it.

Recap of what #1197 fixes: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`'s `_RedactionTracker.record()` used to OR-accumulate a column's "was it shown" state across BOTH `unexpected_index_list` and `partial_unexpected_list`. The fix (already implemented on this branch) makes `redact_sample_failures`/`_RedactionTracker` classify/track against the SAME list the frontend actually displays (dict-shaped `unexpected_index_list` if present, else `partial_unexpected_list`), so the redaction label can no longer undercount vs. what's on screen.

Steps:
1. `conda activate dataq` (never `conda run`).
2. `cd` into the worktree. First `git fetch origin && git merge origin/main` to pick up everything merged since this branch was created (several other PRs in this session's sweep have landed) — resolve conflicts carefully, don't force-push. Re-run the full backend test suite after merging to confirm nothing broke.
3. Run the `/code-review` skill (Skill tool, skill "code-review") against the diff. This touches the redaction/security-sensitive path — take findings seriously. Fix any blocking findings in a follow-up commit and push. File a new GitHub issue for anything genuinely deferred (never drop silently).
4. Wait for CI green after any new push (`gh pr checks 1238 --watch`).
5. Confirm `mergeStateStatus` is CLEAN, then squash-merge: `gh pr merge 1238 --squash --delete-branch`.
6. Confirm `gh issue view 1197` shows closed.

## Task 2: implement and merge #1203 from scratch (fresh branch off updated main)
Run `gh issue view 1203` for full text. Summary: `backend/app/services/run_service.py::_build_result` does `observed = {"error": outcome.error_message} if outcome.error_message else None` for an errored check. `outcome.error_message` is GX's `exception_info.exception_message` passed through verbatim. On a SQL execution engine (Snowflake, and Unity Catalog via #1179), that's typically a SQLAlchemy `StatementError`, whose `str()` appends `[SQL: ...] [parameters: (...)]` — and warehouse cast/conversion errors commonly quote the offending CELL VALUE in the message itself (e.g. "Cannot parse '<value>' as INT"). This lands in `results.observed_value`, which is OUTSIDE the sample_failures retention sweep and OUTSIDE the suite's column-redaction policy — it reaches the run-detail API, UI, alerts, and MCP output completely unredacted. This is the same shape #989 already fixed for monitors (moving a cell value out of the message onto a structured field the read layer can redact).

Fix direction (per the issue, with a clear suggested shape): strip the `[SQL: …] [parameters: …]` tail structurally — SQLAlchemy exposes `.statement`/`.params` separately on `StatementError`, so this is a structural strip (check `orig`/`statement`/`params` attributes), NOT a regex-on-prose hack — keep the driver's own first line of the message. Do NOT apply a blanket `classify_failure_reason`-style scrub (the issue explicitly warns this would regress usability — see `SafeMonitorError`'s docstring for why that distinction was drawn). Must work identically for Snowflake and Unity Catalog (shared gx_runner/run_service path, no per-datasource divergence).

Required test: construct/simulate a `StatementError` carrying a parameter value, run it through `_build_result`, and assert the persisted `observed_value` does NOT contain that parameter value or the `[SQL:`/`[parameters:` tail, but DOES retain the driver's first-line message.

Workflow for task 2:
1. `git checkout main && git pull` then `git checkout -b fix/issue-1203-sql-exception-cell-leak` off up-to-date main (this must happen AFTER task 1's PR #1238 has merged, so branch from main only once that's confirmed in).
2. Implement the fix + test.
3. Run Black/Ruff/mypy + the full affected test files locally, including the existing #1115/#1197/#1190 redaction regression tests to confirm nothing regressed.
4. Commit (conventional commit, `Fixes #1203`, `Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`), push, open PR (use `.github/pull_request_template.md`), milestone matching issue #1203's (`gh issue view 1203 --json milestone`).
5. Run the `/code-review` skill on your diff — security-sensitive path, take findings seriously. Fix blocking findings; file an issue for anything deferred.
6. Wait for CI green, confirm CLEAN merge state, then squash-merge if everything is clean.
7. If code-review or CI surfaces something you're not confident fixing correctly, leave the PR open and say so clearly in your final report rather than merging something shaky.

At the end, report: for both #1197 and #1203 — PR URL, merge status, any follow-up issues filed, and your correctness reasoning for #1203's fix.

input.prompt:
Repo: DataQ (TheurgicDuke771/DataQ). Read CLAUDE.md in the repo root FIRST for the mandatory per-functionality workflow, and note the migration rules ("Backward-compatible migrations only... tested up + down locally").

This branch includes a migration adding `inventory_sync_last_attempted_at`/`inventory_sync_last_error`/`inventory_sync_failing_since` columns to `connections`.

A prior `/code-review` pass on this PR found REAL robustness bugs (not style nits) that must be fixed before merging:

1. **Unguarded `session.commit()` inside the per-connection `except` block in `backend/app/services/inventory_service.py`'s `sync_asset_inventory`** (and the mirrored one in the success `else` branch) — if that bookkeeping commit itself fails (transient Postgres error, deadlock, pool exhaustion), the exception is uncaught and propagates out of the `for connection in connections` loop, aborting the ENTIRE nightly sweep for every remaining connection — violating the function's own documented "one broken connection never starves the rest" fail-soft contract. Wrap these commits in their own try/except that logs and continues rather than propagating.

2. **Missing row-lock on `inventory_sync_failing_since`** — it's currently a plain read-modify-write (`if connection.inventory_sync_failing_since is None: connection.inventory_sync_failing_since = now`) with no `with_for_update()`, a lost-update race under concurrent sweeps. The codebase has an EXACT documented precedent for this: `orchestration_service.record_poll_failure`'s handling of `consecutive_poll_failures`, which explicitly uses `_lock_connection(..., with_for_update=True)` for exactly this reason ("two overlapping sweeps would otherwise both read N, both write N+1 — a lost update"). Read that function and mirror its locking pattern here.

3. **Reading stale/expired ORM attributes after `session.rollback()`** without re-fetching — `session.rollback()` expires all instrumented attributes on the session, and the except block reads `connection.type`/writes back to `connection` immediately after rollback without re-fetching. If the connection row was deleted concurrently (real, reachable path — connection deletion mid-sweep), this raises uncaught `sqlalchemy.orm.exc.ObjectDeletedError`, again aborting the whole sweep. `orchestration_service.record_poll_failure`'s own docstring documents this EXACT hazard in this EXACT codebase and re-fetches the connection by ID inside a fresh transaction rather than reusing the stale ORM instance — mirror that pattern here (re-fetch by connection_id after rollback, handle the "row no longer exists" case gracefully — e.g. skip and log, don't crash the sweep).

4. **`classify_inventory_sync_error`'s broad substring-based PERMISSION classification can misdiagnose unrelated failures** (e.g. a secret-store outage reading the credential BEFORE the warehouse is ever touched) as "missing SELECT grant", sending an admin to fix the wrong thing while the real problem stays undiagnosed. Look at `backend/app/services/failure_classifier.py`'s `classify_inventory_sync_error` — consider whether the classification can be made more precise (e.g. only apply the specific grant-message when the failure demonstrably occurred during warehouse enumeration, not during credential/connection setup), or at minimum make the message hedge appropriately when the category match is broad. Use your judgment on the right level of precision here — perfect disambiguation may not be achievable, but the current blanket substring match is too eager.

5. **Minor (fix if easy, otherwise note):** `inventory_sync_last_error`/`_failing_since` never clear when a connection opts OUT of `inventory_sync` — can go permanently stale if later re-enabled.
